newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish president to meet Pope, discuss NATO.
newsitem.headline: Polish president to meet Pope, discuss NATO.

text.p: Polish President Aleksander Kwasniewski left for a visit to Italy on Sunday to discuss strained relations with the Vatican and seek assurances from the Italian government over the expansion of NATO and European Union.

Kwasniewski, whose ex-communist colleagues from the ruling leftist coalition have been blocking the ratification of a concordat treaty with the Vatican, said he would tackle the issue in talks on Monday with the Polish-born Pope John Paul II.
"I think conditions have now emerged for opponents of the concordat to reconsider their views," Kwasniewski told reporters in Warsaw before his departure.
During his three-day visit he will also meet his Italian counterpart Oscar Scalfaro and Prime Minister Romano Prodi.

Kwasniewski met his political allies from the co-ruling ex-communist Democratic Left Alliance (SLD) on Friday to convince them that the concordat could be ratified after the recent passage of a new constitution, which keeps the state and the church separated.

He said that the SLD, which opposes the concordat on grounds that it would give the Catholic Church too much influence over life in Poland, could now be more willing to back the treaty before parliamentary elections due around September.
"A majority of doubts have been clarified," he said.
The concordat was signed in 1993 by the then right-centrist, pro-Church government, just before the ex-communists and a peasant party won parliamentary elections.
Relations between Warsaw and the Vatican have also been clouded by a liberalised abortion law, which Kwasniewski signed last year despite protests from the Pope.
Kwasniewski and John Paul are also widely expected to discuss the Pontiff's 11-day trip to Poland starting on May 31.
Many analysts say the pope's pilgrimage is likely to boost the chances of rightist parties in the coming elections.
The Pontiff is widely believed to have provided much of the spiritual inspiration for the Solidarity movement to overthrow communism in 1989.
Kwasniewski said he would also seek Italy's unconditional support for NATO's plans to recruit new east European members from the former Soviet bloc, despite Russia's strong opposition.

The Polish news media have widely publicised statements by some Italian politicians, notably Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini, that Moscow should have a say over the expansion of the western military alliance.

"I shall try to convince Italian politicians that there should be no ambiguity over the issue. Making Russia's consent a condition to it (NATO expansion) would in reality block new members' entry to the pact," Kwasniewski said.
